### Executive Signal
- The dominant debate today is **open-source versus [proprietary AI](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-afe4276bf491)**: **Yann LeCun** accuses closed labs of absorbing open research without contributing back, while **Timnit Gebru** calls anti-open-source criticism corporate propaganda. This dispute frames how the community currently weighs transparency, safety, competition, and who benefits from AI progress.

### Priority Developments
- **Neel Nanda**, a leading mechanistic interpretability researcher, highlighted work [using phantom transfer as a proxy task](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-9e1217d3da58) to test whether data-attribution techniques can trace subtle traits models inherit via distillation. It is shared as promising ongoing technical work, not peer-reviewed conclusions.
- **Jason Wei** of OpenAI argued [that verifiability is a](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-83d1841b700b) spectrum, claiming even "non-verifiable" tasks can be judged by experts or market signals. This is clearly opinion rather than evidence, but it engages a trending evaluation question.
- **Jerry Liu**, LlamaIndex founder, flagged **OCRia-nano-1**, an 8.1M-parameter OCR model handling [scanned text](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-b77964ae2e6a), tables, and multiple languages, and **Santiago Valdarrama** broke down **LingBot-Map 2.0** for online camera-pose estimation and 3D scene reconstruction. Both are concrete, checkable technical claims.
- **Greg Brockman** announced **Private Inference**, a confidential-computing capability [with strict controls over prompts and responses](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-ecdab81b4811) during processing, currently in testing. The announcement carries authority but the capability itself is not yet independently evaluated.
- **@tunguz** described a months-long collaboration with a mathematics professor using **Astra** on long-standing open problems, citing public artifacts as evidence; this is an original first-hand account of frontier models aiding serious research.

### Leadership Implications
- The open-versus-closed fight and **Gebru**'s critique of the **Pangram** detection tool show rising reputational risk around unverifiable AI claims. Teams should track the policy debate and demand reliability evidence before deploying detection, attribution, or moderation tooling on real users.
- Watch adoption and engineering signals: **Perplexity Teammates** reportedly [doubling every ten](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-5fbed379769d) days among $200/month users is an early demand indicator for paid agent products, while **Kent C. Dodds**' temporary-verification-test pattern offers a practical template for keeping agentic codebases maintainable.

items.content:
Imagine a robot walking in a museum and mapping everything it sees.

The robot uses every camera frame to estimate where it is and build a 3D representation.

But generating a good map is hard: every small error can accumulate as the robot moves, causing the map to gradually drift out of alignment.

@robbyant_brain addresses this with LingBot-Map 2.0:

It's a model that takes video and estimates the camera's path and the scene's 3D geometry frame by frame.

This version has a new feature: Refine, and the way it works is pretty cool:

• Refine updates the geometric context the model uses to estimate the camera trajectory.

• It saves those updates to the model so it can improve existing reconstructions and use the updated geometry to process future frames.

• You can trigger Refine at any point during a run to reduce accumulated drift.

And all of this happens inside the model, without any external optimization backend.

Look at the attached demo:

• The orange path is the estimated camera trajectory before Refine.
• The cyan path shows the corrected trajectory after Refine.

This is one of the key capabilities supporting the embodied-native, general-purpose robot brain @robbyant_brain is building. Without reliable spatial memory, autonomous work over large areas and long hours isn't possible.

Here is more information about the model:

• Project page: https://technology.robbyant.com/lingbot-map-v2

• Technical report: https://github.com/Robbyant/lingbot-map-v2/blob/main/docs/lingbot-map-v2_paper.pdf

• GitHub: https://github.com/Robbyant/lingbot-map-v2

• Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/robbyant/lingbot-map-v2

The Streaming version is open source; Refine is not included.

Solving problems in his speciality that have been open for decades or even longer. We are having a blast. He and his other collaborators are well established in their jobs, not seeking to climb any more academic career ladders. I am completely outside the academic professional/status games, and am just grateful to be learning about something new and pushing the envelope of knowledge for its own sake. items.title: A lot of business owners, founders and CEOs now need to have the difficult conversation with themsel...
items.content:
A lot of business owners, founders and CEOs now need to have the difficult conversation with themselves that their business simply doesn't have a reason to exist anymore in this new era

I think the types of businesses (and people) that succeed in a post-AGI era might just be completely different

You understand better now the extremely aggressive pivots to AI many companies a few years ago did, completely resetting their company or rebuilding it from scratch after they realized this

I remember Replit for example was just an online IDE that you could use with other people (targeted to coders), it got big with coding teachers, then in 2024 @amasad hard pivoted it to be an AI app and site generator target to the opposite audience: non-coders, which caused lots of backlash, but that worked, now it's projected to hit $1B ARR by end of this year!

Anyway, we're in a completely new era with completely different dynamics for what businesses will survive and which will perish, what worked last year might not work this year anymore, and what works this year might not work next year anymore, because we're dealing with AI models that get exponentially better every year

items.content:
Let me try to explain why I'm in favor of blocking AI replies, and I love what @levelsio is doing. 

I'll answer every single one of your points:

> "The cure is worse than the disease."

I gave up on my comment section a few months ago because AI replies ran it over. Since I started blocking these spammers aggressively, I can now read real humans again.

This cure is way better *to me* than the disease.  You don't have to participate or like it, but this has improved my experience on this platform by 200%.

> A public blocklist fed by anyone tagging a bot turns every thread into a tribunal

The list doesn't automatically add the accounts you report. First, every account gets verified, and it's only marked as spam after many AI-looking replies.

If an account is reported and that person doesn't post AI-generated slop, the account will never be added to the block list.

> accusations with no due process

This is not the case. Even if you get added to the blocklist, you can request removal, and you will, as long as you stop posting AI-generated slop.

> and real people listed as "AI spammers" for life

Again, this isn't true for the reasons I explained above.

> AI replies are annoying

No, they aren't just annoying; they are literally the death of this platform.

> A crowd hunting them is dangerous.

It is dangerous! To those ruining this for everyone else.

items.title: If I have Bluetooth enabled on my MacBook Pro, Chrome will request a list of paired Bluetooth device...
items.content:
If I have Bluetooth enabled on my MacBook Pro, Chrome will request a list of paired Bluetooth devices 27 times per second, freezing my computer every 3 seconds

About 15,000+ requests per minute

This is Chrome 158.0.8127.37

@ChromiumDev 

From my clanker: "Chrome is doing the same thing I found on Nov 11, and it's happening right now. It isn't caused by your superlevels extension, which has no Bluetooth code.

What I measured just now (30 seconds of the Bluetooth service's log):
- Chrome asked macOS for your list of paired devices about 27 times a second.
- It asked for the state of individual devices about 190 times a second, roughly 7 devices on every pass.
- That's about 15,000+ requests from Chrome per minute. Every other app combined sent about 60.
- bluetoothd, the macOS Bluetooth service, is at 59% CPU because of it.

Why Chrome does this: Chrome keeps track of paired Bluetooth devices for passkey sign-in with your phone and for websites that connect to Bluetooth devices. Normally it checks every so often. Here it's stuck in a loop and checks dozens of times a second. No extension or Chrome flag is causing it, so it looks like a Chrome bug. On Nov 11 it started right after a Bluetooth device disconnected, and it has probably been stuck again since a disconnect at some point. Chrome has been running for 4.5 days."
